blocks.content: Earthquakes and volcanoes are powerful endogenic forces originating from within the Earth. They are direct outcomes of plate tectonic movements and provide vital evidence about the Earth’s interior, crustal structure, and dynamic nature of the planet. This chapter is extremely important for SSC examinations because questions are asked from definitions, causes, terminology, types, global distribution, effects, and preventive measures.
PART A: EARTHQUAKES

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Earthquake origination involves faulting, distinguishing between the internal Focus (Hypocentre) and surface Epicentre.
Seismic waves are divided into two main categories: Body Waves (P and S waves) and Surface Waves.
Volcanoes are categorized based on both their eruptive activity (active, dormant, extinct) and physical shape.
Earthquakes and volcanoes share global geographical distributions along major tectonic belts.
Study of earthquake mitigation, measurement, and preparedness is critical for reducing hazard impacts.

blocks.content: Meaning of Earthquake

An earthquake is a sudden shaking or vibration of the Earth’s surface caused by the release of stored energy in the Earth’s crust. This energy accumulates due to continuous movement of tectonic plates. When stress exceeds the strength of rocks, the rocks break along fault lines, releasing energy in the form of seismic waves.
Causes of Earthquakes

The primary cause of earthquakes is tectonic movement along faults. As plates move, friction prevents smooth motion and stress builds up. When this stress is suddenly released, earthquakes occur. Secondary causes include volcanic eruptions, collapse of underground caverns, landslides, reservoir-induced seismicity due to large dams, mining activities, and underground nuclear explosions.
Faults and Earthquakes

A fault is a fracture or zone of weakness in the Earth’s crust along which displacement occurs. Most earthquakes originate along faults. Major fault types include normal faults, reverse faults, and strike-slip faults. Transform plate boundaries are typically associated with strike-slip faults.
Focus (Hypocentre) and Epicentre

The focus, also called the hypocentre, is the point inside the Earth where the earthquake originates. The epicentre is the point on the Earth’s surface directly above the focus. Seismic energy is strongest near the epicentre, and damage decreases with distance from it.
Seismic Waves
Seismic waves are energy waves produced by earthquakes and travel outward from the focus. They are classified into body waves and surface waves.
Body Waves

Body waves travel through the Earth’s interior and are of two types. P-waves (Primary waves) are compressional waves that move particles parallel to the direction of wave travel. They are the fastest waves and can pass through solids, liquids, and gases. S-waves (Secondary waves) are transverse waves in which particles move perpendicular to the direction of wave travel. They are slower than P-waves and can travel only through solid materials. Their absence in the outer core proves that the outer core is liquid.
Surface Waves

Surface waves travel along the Earth’s surface and have the highest amplitude. They cause maximum destruction because their energy is concentrated near the surface. They are responsible for severe damage to buildings and infrastructure.
Measurement of Earthquakes

Earthquakes are measured using different scales. The Richter Scale measures the magnitude or energy released by an earthquake and is logarithmic in nature. The Mercalli Intensity Scale measures the intensity of an earthquake based on observed damage and human experience.
Earthquake Belts of the World

Earthquakes are not randomly distributed. Most earthquakes occur along plate boundaries. The Circum-Pacific Belt, also known as the Ring of Fire, is the most active earthquake zone. The Alpine-Himalayan Belt extends from Southern Europe to Southeast Asia. Another important belt is along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Effects of Earthquakes

Earthquakes can cause severe loss of life and property. Primary effects include ground shaking and surface rupture. Secondary effects include landslides, tsunamis, fires, liquefaction of soil, and disruption of transport and communication systems.
Earthquake Preparedness and Mitigation

Earthquake hazards can be reduced through proper planning and preparedness. Earthquake- resistant construction, land-use planning, public awareness, early warning systems, and disaster management strategies play a vital role in minimizing losses.
PART B: VOLCANOES

rows: Based on Activity & Based on Shape

blocks.content: Meaning of Volcano

A volcano is an opening or vent in the Earth’s crust through which molten magma, volcanic gases, and ash escape to the surface. Volcanic activity provides direct evidence of the Earth’s interior processes.
Causes of Volcanic Eruptions
Volcanic eruptions occur when magma rises towards the surface due to intense heat and pressure. Weak zones in the Earth’s crust, plate boundaries, and hotspots allow magma to escape.
Subduction zones and divergent boundaries are major sites of volcanic activity.
Types of Volcanoes Based on Activity

Active volcanoes erupt frequently or have erupted in recent times. Dormant volcanoes remain inactive for long periods but may erupt again. Extinct volcanoes have no record of eruption in historical times and are unlikely to erupt.
Types of Volcanoes Based on Shape

Shield volcanoes are formed by fluid lava and have broad, gentle slopes. Composite or stratovolcanoes are formed by alternating layers of lava and ash and are highly explosive. Cinder cone volcanoes are small, steep-sided volcanoes formed from volcanic fragments.
Distribution of Volcanoes

items: SSC questions frequently ask to differentiate between Focus (Hypocentre) and Epicentre.
Be prepared for direct questions regarding the classification of Body Waves vs Surface Waves.
Memorize types of volcanoes based on shape and activity as they are common SSC targets.

blocks.content: Volcanoes are unevenly distributed across the globe. The majority of volcanoes are found along the Circum-Pacific Belt. Some volcanoes occur away from plate boundaries at hotspots, such as the Hawaiian Islands.
Effects of Volcanic Eruptions
Volcanic eruptions have both destructive and constructive effects. Destructive effects include loss of life, destruction of settlements, air pollution, and climatic cooling due to volcanic ash.
Constructive effects include formation of fertile soils, new landforms, and mineral deposits.
Importance of Studying Earthquakes and Volcanoes

The study of earthquakes and volcanoes is essential for understanding plate tectonics, Earth’s interior, and natural hazards. It helps in disaster risk reduction, urban planning, and sustainable development.
